uncited: ConeBeamGeometry defines the physical and geometric parameters for a cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) acquisition, specifically for systems where the X-ray source and detector move along a trajectory (typically circular) relative to the object.

It serves as the foundational data structure for the [Arbitrary Source-Detector Geometry Projector](2975-arbitrary-source-detector-geometry-projector.md), providing the fixed distances and detector dimensions required to map 3D world coordinates to 2D detector pixels.
Unlike standard parallel-beam assumptions, this model accounts for the divergent nature of the X-ray beam, requiring precise magnification factors to relate voxel sizes to detector bin sizes.
*   **Inputs:** Physical scanner specifications (distances, pixel size), acquisition trajectory (angles), and detector array dimensions.
**Projection Magnification ($\alpha$):** Relates the source-detector distance to the detector bin size.
**Isosampling Magnification ($t_z$):** Relates the source-isocenter distance to the voxel size at the isocenter.
Where $t_z^{\text{voxel}}$ is the physical voxel size at the center of rotation.
*   Focal spot to detector distance (DSD): 1295 mm
*   Focal spot to rotation center (DSO): 820 mm
*   Field of View (FOV): 65 mm (for a $512 \times 512$ detector)
The following Python-like pseudocode initializes the geometry object and computes the necessary magnification factors.
It assumes standard vector operations are available.
*   **Voxel Size Mismatch:** Using a larger voxel size (e.g., 0.508 mm vs 0.127 mm) to increase FOV degrades resolution.
*   **Time Complexity:** The geometry setup itself is $O(1)$ or $O(N_{angles})$ for angle generation.
The computational cost lies in the subsequent projection/backprojection steps, which are $O(N_{voxels} \cdot N_{angles})$ for direct methods.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N_{angles} \cdot N_{det\_pixels}^2)$ to store projection data.
Supports variable FOV by adjusting voxel size relative to magnification factors.
Computationally expensive for large volumes and high-resolution detectors.
*   **When to use:** When reconstructing data from a CBCT scanner (e.g., C-arm systems) where the source and detector move in a circular or helical trajectory.
*   **When not to use:** For parallel-beam CT or when using simplified fan-beam approximations where cone-beam artifacts are negligible.
Cone-beam CT geometry originated with the development of C-arm X-ray systems for interventional radiology and dental imaging.
The geometry is a critical component in algorithms like the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, which approximates the exact cone-beam reconstruction.

This directly supports the claim that the distinction between these two magnification factors highlights the challenge of balancing field of view and resolution.
